title: Is There Evidence for the Development of Sex-Specific Guidelines for Ultramarathon Coaches and Athletes? A Systematic Review
population: 45 studies comparing male and female elite and recreational ultramarathon runners.
findings: PRISMA review; 45 studies met inclusion; most observational, only three based on randomised controlled trials.
Overall quality of evidence was low (GRADE).

Sex differences were found in predictors of ultramarathon performance, physiological responses to training, racing and recovery, health issues and pacing; some findings contradictory and very few studied specific interventions.

Most advice for ultramarathons is based on research that largely excluded female athletes; authors conclude sex-specific guidelines could affect performance and health of female runners but there is insufficient high-quality evidence to formulate them.
limitations: Low-quality primary evidence; no training-dose recommendations or long-run values in the abstract.
implications: Any ultra long-run numbers are extrapolated largely from male samples; state this limitation in the rule notes instead of applying sex-specific values.

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (Sports Med Open, 2023-01-25, Kelly) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 36695958). 45 studies, three RCT-based, GRADE low match. Kept for the extrapolation caveat only.
